title: Best Beer for No Hangover: Light Lagers vs IPAs vs Stouts
excerpt: Which beer gives you the least hangover? Beer styles ranked by hangover risk, why strength beats brand, light vs dark, IPAs, stouts, and how to drink beer smarter.
metaDescription: Which beer gives the least hangover? Light lagers, IPAs, and stouts ranked by hangover risk, plus why alcohol strength matters more than the brand.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** no beer is hangover-free, but some make a rough morning much less likely. The single biggest factor is not the brand or the style. It's how much alcohol is in each glass and how many glasses you drink. A light lager at around 4% alcohol gives your body far less to deal with than a 9% double IPA or an imperial stout poured in the same size glass. After strength, the smaller factors are color and complexity (pale, clean, filtered beers tend to carry fewer of the by-products linked to worse hangovers), carbonation and pace, and whether you personally react to something in beer, like gluten or histamine.

**The quick picks:** if you want the lowest hangover risk while still drinking real beer, choose a light lager, a session beer (under about 4.5% alcohol), a classic pilsner, or a kölsch. Swap every second or third beer for a non-alcoholic one. Treat IPAs, Belgian ales, barrel-aged stouts, and anything labeled "double," "imperial," or "tripel" as two drinks per glass, because they often are.

> **A quick safety note.** This guide is for adults who drink socially and want to feel better the next day. It isn't medical advice. If you take medication, are pregnant, have a liver, kidney, or heart condition, or have ever had a bad reaction to beer (hives, wheezing, swelling), talk to your doctor before drinking. If someone is confused, vomiting repeatedly, breathing slowly, or hard to wake after drinking, that's a possible sign of alcohol poisoning. Call 911 (or your local emergency number) and don't leave them alone.

## Why Some Beers Leave You Worse Off Than Others

A hangover is your body's reaction to a night of alcohol. Researchers still argue about the exact causes, but the main players are well known: poorer sleep, dehydration and lost electrolytes, irritation of the stomach lining, a low-grade inflammatory response, and the build-up of **acetaldehyde**, a toxic chemical your liver makes while it breaks alcohol down. All of those scale with the total amount of alcohol you drink.

That's why the most useful question to ask about any beer is "how much alcohol am I actually getting?" Everything else is a smaller adjustment on top. If you want the full picture of why beer mornings feel the way they do (heavy, bloated, foggy rather than sharp), our [beer hangover guide](/never-hungover/beer-hangover) goes deep on it. This page is the shopping side: what to pick at the bar or the store.

### Strength: the factor that matters most

Beer ranges from under 0.5% alcohol (non-alcoholic) to well over 10%. In the US, one standard drink is about 14 grams of pure alcohol, which the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA) equates to 12 ounces of regular beer at about 5% alcohol. A lot of modern beer is much stronger than that, and it's often served in bigger glasses.

Here's a simple way to do the math. Multiply the ounces in the glass by the alcohol percentage, then divide by 0.6. The answer is roughly how many standard drinks you're holding.

| Beer and pour | Approx. alcohol | Standard drinks |
|---|---|---|
| 12 oz light lager | 4.2% | about 0.8 |
| 12 oz regular lager | 5% | about 1.0 |
| 16 oz pint of pilsner | 4.5% | about 1.2 |
| 16 oz pint of IPA | 7% | about 1.9 |
| 16 oz pint of double IPA | 9% | about 2.4 |
| 12 oz imperial stout | 11% | about 2.2 |

Look at the gap between the top and the bottom of that table. Four pints of double IPA is close to ten standard drinks. Four light lagers is a bit over three. Same number of glasses, completely different morning. This is the main reason people say "IPAs give me worse hangovers." In many cases they're simply drinking a lot more alcohol than they think. (We cover the other possible reasons in our [IPA hangover guide](/never-hungover/ipa-hangover).)

### Congeners: a smaller but real effect

Congeners are by-products of fermentation and aging, such as certain alcohols other than ethanol, aldehydes, and other flavor compounds. Darker, more complex drinks generally carry more of them. The best-known study on this, by Rohsenow and colleagues (published in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research* in 2010), found that bourbon, which is high in congeners, produced worse hangovers than vodka at the same alcohol level. The difference was real but modest, and the alcohol dose mattered more.

Beer as a category is lower in congeners than dark spirits like whiskey or brandy, and the differences between beer styles haven't been measured as carefully. As a reasonable rule, a pale, filtered lager is "cleaner" than a dark, strong, barrel-aged beer, but don't expect color alone to save you. Our guide to [congeners in alcohol](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol) explains which drinks carry the most.

### Carbonation and pace

Bubbles may help alcohol reach your bloodstream a little faster. A small study by Roberts and Robinson (2007) found that carbonated drinks raised blood alcohol faster than flat ones in most participants, although people varied. Beer is also easy to drink quickly when it's cold and fizzy, especially in a group where rounds keep coming. Faster drinking means higher peaks, worse sleep, and a harder morning.

### Personal sensitivities

Some people react to things in beer beyond the alcohol: gluten from barley and wheat, histamine and other amines that can form during fermentation, or specific ingredients like certain hops or yeast. If you get headaches, flushing, a stuffy nose, or stomach trouble from beer but not from the same amount of wine or spirits, that's a clue. Our guides to [beer headaches](/never-hungover/beer-headache) and [histamine intolerance and alcohol](/never-hungover/histamine-intolerance-and-alcohol) can help you narrow it down.

## Light Lagers vs IPAs vs Stouts: Beer Styles Ranked for Hangover Risk

This ranking puts the most common styles in rough order, from lowest to highest typical hangover risk. It's based mostly on typical alcohol content, with a nudge for congeners and how the beer is usually served. Individual beers vary a lot, so always check the label.

### 1. Non-alcoholic beer (lowest risk)

Beer labeled non-alcoholic in the US can still contain up to 0.5% alcohol, and some "alcohol-free" products go lower. At that level, a normal amount won't give a typical adult a hangover. Mixing a few into a night out is one of the most effective things you can do. If you're curious about the edge cases, see [can non-alcoholic beer give you a hangover](/never-hungover/non-alcoholic-beer-hangover).

### 2. Light lagers and "ultra" beers

Mainstream light beers such as Michelob Ultra, Bud Light, Miller Lite, and Coors Light are typically around 4.2% alcohol in the US (strength can differ in other countries). They're pale, filtered, and low in congeners. Their real advantage is that each can carries less alcohol than a regular beer, so a night of them adds up more slowly.

The downside: they're easy to drink fast, and "light" refers to calories more than alcohol. Some light beers are close to regular strength. Don't assume, check the can.

### 3. Session beers (under about 4.5%)

"Session" means a beer meant to be drunk over a long session without getting you too drunk too fast. Session IPAs, English bitters and milds, and lighter pale ales often sit between 3% and 4.7%. They give you more flavor than a light lager with a similar alcohol load. A British-style bitter at 3.8% is a very different night from an American IPA at 7%.

### 4. Pilsner, helles, and kölsch

Classic pale lagers are clean, crisp, and usually between about 4.4% and 5%. Pilsner Urquell, for example, is about 4.4%. A kölsch from Cologne is typically around 4.8% and traditionally served in small glasses, which naturally slows you down. These are a good middle ground if light beer tastes too thin to you.

### 5. Standard lagers

Everyday lagers such as Budweiser or Heineken are around 5%. That's the "one standard drink" benchmark. Nothing special for or against hangovers here. The count is what matters.

### 6. Dry stouts (a surprise entry)

Guinness Draught looks heavy, but it's only about 4.2% alcohol, similar to a light beer. Dark color doesn't mean high strength. A dry Irish stout poured on nitro is also less fizzy and drinks more slowly than a cold lager. It carries more roasted-malt compounds than a pale beer, but if you're choosing between a pint of Guinness and a pint of 7% IPA, the stout is the gentler choice by a wide margin.

### 7. Wheat beers and hefeweizens

German-style wheat beers are usually 5% to 5.5% and often unfiltered, so they contain yeast and more wheat protein. Some people find these sit heavily on the stomach. They're also commonly served in half-liter glasses (about 17 ounces), which means one glass can be closer to 1.5 standard drinks. Fine in moderation, but count by the glass size.

### 8. Pale ales and amber ales

American pale ales and ambers typically run 5% to 6%. Sierra Nevada Pale Ale, a classic of the style, is about 5.6%. Slightly more alcohol than a lager, and the hops and caramel malts add some complexity. A reasonable choice if you keep count.

### 9. IPAs

The standard American IPA is usually 6% to 7.5%, and a lot of popular hazy IPAs sit in that range too. Hazy and unfiltered IPAs also carry more yeast and hop material. Two pints of a 7% IPA is close to four standard drinks. If you love IPAs, the best move is to look for session IPAs (around 4% to 5%) or to alternate with something lighter.

### 10. Sours and fruited beers

These vary wildly, from 3% Berliner weisse to 8% or more for heavily fruited "smoothie" sours. Some contain added sugar or fruit purée. There's no strong evidence that sugar itself causes hangovers, but sweet, tart beers are easy to drink quickly and can mask how strong they are. Check the label.

### 11. Belgian strong ales, tripels, and quads

Belgian strong ales are often 8% to 11%. They're delicious and deceptively smooth, and they're often served in goblets that hold 11 to 13 ounces. One glass can be two standard drinks. These beers also tend to be rich in fermentation by-products from their characteristic yeasts.

### 12. Double IPAs, imperial stouts, and barrel-aged beers (highest risk)

Anything labeled "double," "imperial," or "barrel-aged" usually lands between 8% and 14%. Barrel-aged stouts also pick up compounds from the wood and the spirit that was in the barrel, much like a dark liquor. These are beers to sip, share, or save for a small pour. A few of them can match the alcohol of a night of shots.

## Best Beers for No Hangover: Practical Picks by Situation

Rather than a list of brands to buy, here's what to reach for depending on where you are.

- **At a sports bar or barbecue:** a light lager or "ultra" beer, with a water or non-alcoholic beer between rounds. Low alcohol per can and easy to count.
- **At a craft brewery:** ask for the session beer, pilsner, kölsch, or the lowest-ABV option on the board. Many breweries list alcohol percentages next to each beer. Order smaller pours (many offer 8 to 10 ounce glasses or flights) for anything over 6%.
- **At an Irish pub:** a dry stout like Guinness at around 4.2% is a better pick than most of the taps around it.
- **At a beer festival:** small tasting pours are the norm, but they add up fast. Keep a rough count, drink water between tastings, and eat.
- **At home:** stock a mix of regular and non-alcoholic beer so the easy default is to alternate.
- **If gluten bothers you:** look for beers brewed from gluten-free grains like sorghum, rice, or millet. "Gluten-reduced" beers are brewed with barley and treated with an enzyme, and they aren't considered safe for people with celiac disease. Our [gluten-free alcohol guide](/never-hungover/gluten-free-alcohol) explains the difference.

## Does Light Beer Give You Less of a Hangover?

Usually yes, but only because of the alcohol. Drink by drink, a 4.2% light beer carries about 15% to 20% less alcohol than a 5% regular lager, and far less than a strong craft beer. Light beers are also pale and filtered, so they're low in congeners.

The catch is that people often drink more of them. If light beer means you have eight instead of five, you've given most of the advantage back. Light beer helps when you keep the count the same and let the lower strength do its work.

## Is Dark Beer Worse for Hangovers Than Light Beer?

Not automatically. Darkness in beer comes from roasted malt, not alcohol. A dry stout can be weaker than a pale IPA. Darker beers do generally contain more roasted-malt compounds, and in theory that could add a little to hangover severity, but the evidence comparing beer styles directly is thin. What's well established is that the strong, dark beers (imperial stouts, barrel-aged porters, Belgian quads) are high in alcohol, and that's what does the damage.

So the practical rule is: judge a dark beer by its ABV, not its color.

## Which Beer Has the Fewest Congeners?

As a general rule, pale, filtered, lower-strength lagers have the fewest. Light lagers, pilsners, helles, and kölsch sit at the "clean" end. Unfiltered, hazy, high-strength, and barrel-aged beers sit at the other end. Precise congener levels vary by brewery and batch and aren't printed on labels, so treat this as a sensible rule of thumb rather than a guarantee.

It's also worth keeping congeners in perspective. Even in the bourbon versus vodka study, the gap was modest. If you drink a lot of a low-congener beer, you'll still have a hangover.

## Draft vs Bottled vs Canned: Does It Matter?

For hangovers, the package itself makes little difference. The main thing that changes is the size of the pour. A bottle or can is usually 12 ounces, while a draft pint is often 16 ounces in the US and about 20 ounces in the UK. Pour size can quietly add a third more alcohol per round.

Some people do report headaches from draft beer at certain bars. Dirty draft lines are a real issue in the beer world, and old or poorly kept beer can taste off, but there's no good evidence linking draft lines to hangovers specifically. If you're curious, see our piece on [draft beer headaches](/never-hungover/draft-beer-headache).

## Does Mixing Beer With Other Drinks Make It Worse?

The old saying "beer before liquor, never sicker" doesn't hold up. A 2019 study by Köchling and colleagues in the *American Journal of Clinical Nutrition* gave volunteers beer then wine, wine then beer, or one drink only, and found the order made no meaningful difference to hangover severity. What mattered was how much people drank and how drunk they felt.

Mixing drinks can still lead to a worse night indirectly, because switching between beer, wine, and shots makes it harder to keep count. More on that in our [beer before liquor myth](/never-hungover/beer-before-liquor-myth) breakdown.

## Beer vs Other Drinks: Where Beer Sits on the Hangover Scale

Ounce for ounce, beer is one of the weaker drinks you can order, and it tends to be lower in congeners than dark spirits. That's the good news. The bad news is that it's served in large volumes and drunk over long nights, which is how people end up drinking more total alcohol than they would with a couple of cocktails.

If you're comparing across categories, our ranking of the [least hangover-causing alcohol](/never-hungover/least-hangover-alcohol-ranked) puts beer in context with wine and spirits. If spirits are your thing, the same principles apply to choosing a [tequila with less of a hangover](/never-hungover/best-tequila-for-no-hangover): lower strength per serving, cleaner production, and a slower pace.

## How to Drink Beer Without Wrecking Tomorrow

Picking the right beer is half the job. The other half is how you drink it.

1. **Check the ABV before you order.** It takes five seconds and is the most useful number on the menu.
2. **Count in standard drinks, not glasses.** A pint of 7% IPA is about two drinks. A goblet of Belgian tripel is about two.
3. **Alternate with water or non-alcoholic beer.** It slows your pace and helps with fluid loss. Your body clears roughly one standard drink an hour, and nothing you drink speeds that up.
4. **Eat a real meal first.** Food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol is absorbed. Protein, fat, and fiber help most.
5. **Choose smaller pours for strong beer.** Half pints, 10 ounce glasses, and tasting flights all help.
6. **Stop an hour or two before bed.** Alcohol close to bedtime disrupts deep sleep and REM sleep, which is a big part of why you feel wrecked the next day.
7. **Rehydrate before sleep.** A glass or two of water, and an electrolyte drink if you've had a lot. See our guide to [electrolytes and alcohol](/never-hungover/electrolytes-and-alcohol).

For a complete plan, read [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## When a "Beer Hangover" Might Be Something Else

Most rough beer mornings are ordinary hangovers. A few patterns are worth taking seriously.

> **When to see a doctor.** Get checked if beer (even a small amount) regularly gives you hives, a rash, swelling of the lips or face, wheezing, or severe stomach pain, since that can be an allergy or intolerance to an ingredient like wheat, barley, or hops. If you have celiac disease, beer brewed from barley or wheat isn't safe, including most "gluten-reduced" beer. See a doctor if your hangovers are getting much worse over time, if you get shaky, sweaty, or anxious when you haven't had a drink, or if you need a drink in the morning to feel normal. Those can be signs that your body has become dependent on alcohol, and a doctor can help you cut back safely. **Call 911 right away** if someone is confused, can't stay awake, is vomiting repeatedly, has slow or irregular breathing, or has blue-tinged or very pale skin.

## Where DHM Fits In

Choosing lighter beer and drinking at a slower pace are the most reliable ways to protect tomorrow. Some people also use dihydromyricetin (DHM), a compound from the Japanese raisin tree, as part of their routine on a beer-heavy night.

The research on DHM is promising but early. A 2012 study in the *Journal of Neuroscience* (Shen and colleagues) found DHM reduced alcohol intoxication effects and withdrawal signs in rats, and later animal work has looked at its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Good human trials are still limited, so there is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers in people, and it does nothing to make a 10% beer safer to drink quickly. Think of it as an optional extra, not a license to drink more.

If you want to try it, two options we've reviewed are [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), a simple, low-cost single-ingredient tablet, and [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), which adds L-cysteine and electrolytes at a higher price per serving. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers timing and amounts, and you can compare more products in our [supplement reviews](/reviews). If you take any regular medication, check with your doctor or pharmacist first.

## The Bottom Line

The best beer for avoiding a hangover is a lower-alcohol one, drunk slowly, with food and water in between. Light lagers, session beers, pilsners, kölsch, and even a dry stout like Guinness all sit around 4% to 5%. IPAs, Belgian strong ales, double IPAs, and imperial or barrel-aged stouts often pack two drinks into one glass. Color matters less than strength, the brand matters less than the count, and swapping in non-alcoholic beer for part of the night helps more than any label claim.

Curious about the dark-beer exception people always ask about? Our [Guinness hangover](/never-hungover/guinness-hangover) guide explains why a stout can be lighter on alcohol than it looks.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What beer gives you the least hangover?**

Lower-alcohol, pale, filtered beers give you the best odds: light lagers, session beers, pilsners, and kölsch, usually between about 4% and 5% alcohol. Non-alcoholic beer is the lowest-risk option of all. The amount you drink still matters more than the beer you pick.

**Does light beer give you less of a hangover?**

Usually, because each can contains less alcohol (often around 4.2% versus 5% for a regular lager) and light beers are low in congeners. The benefit disappears if you end up drinking more cans because they feel lighter. Keep the count the same and the lower strength works in your favor.

**Are IPAs worse for hangovers?**

Often, mainly because most IPAs are 6% to 7.5% alcohol and double IPAs can reach 9% or more, so each pint holds close to two standard drinks or more. Hazy and unfiltered IPAs also carry more yeast and hop material, which some people find harder on the stomach. Session IPAs around 4% to 5% are a good compromise.

**Is Guinness or stout worse for a hangover than lager?**

Not necessarily. Guinness Draught is only about 4.2% alcohol, similar to a light beer, and it's less fizzy. Imperial and barrel-aged stouts are a different story at 8% to 14% alcohol. Judge a dark beer by its alcohol percentage, not its color.

**Does mixing beer and liquor cause a worse hangover?**

The order you drink in doesn't seem to matter. A 2019 study in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition found that drinking beer before wine, or wine before beer, made no meaningful difference to hangover severity. The total amount of alcohol is what counts, and mixing drinks can make it harder to keep track of that.

**Can non-alcoholic beer give you a hangover?**

For a typical adult, normal amounts won't. US non-alcoholic beer can contain up to 0.5% alcohol, which is far too little to cause a hangover at ordinary quantities. Some people may still feel bloated or get a headache from other ingredients, but that's not a true hangover.

**Is gluten-free beer better for hangovers?**

Only if gluten bothers you. For people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity, beer brewed from gluten-free grains can avoid symptoms that pile on top of a hangover. For everyone else, there is no good evidence that gluten-free beer causes a milder hangover at the same alcohol level.

**Does DHM help with beer hangovers?**

There is no good evidence from human trials that DHM prevents hangovers. Animal research on DHM and alcohol is promising, and some people include it in their routine. It doesn't replace the basics: lower-alcohol beer, food, water, a slower pace, and stopping well before bed.
